body:
`case_study:pc-jeweller-2018` | 2018-05-04 | tickers: PCJEWELLER | confidence: verified

PC Jeweller hit a high of ~Rs 600 on 16 Jan 2018 (pre-2024 split prices), fell 42% in a month during the Feb 2018 Nirav Modi/PNB jewellery-sector contagion, then crashed again in Apr-May 2018 when the promoter gifted shares to family members via off-market transfers (~$2.7 bn of m-cap lost at the worst point). A buyback announced to calm markets was withdrawn in Jul 2018 (-43% in a week to ~Rs 68). Mid-2018 low ~Rs 95 then further to the teens/single digits by 2020; the company defaulted on ~Rs 3,400-3,466 cr of bank loans (2021-22) and SBI sought insolvency. A 2024 settlement with lenders sparked a speculative rally. Visible flags: (1) inventory and receivables (export receivables, UAE) rising much faster than sales; CFO weak or negative for years despite reported profits; (2) heavy gold-metal-loan/working-capital debt; (3) links to Vakrangee (itself under SEBI scrutiny), which held PCJ shares; (4) promoter share 'gifts' and poor disclosure; (5) buyback withdrawal = management credibility loss. Lesson: in jewellery, inventory days and receivable days are the forensic key; a gold retailer reporting profits but no cash is suspect. Insolvency-adjacent rallies are not turnarounds until debt is actually extinguished.

**Lesson:** Inventory + receivable days decide jewellery quality
**Spotted early by:** market sellers after promoter gift disclosure
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:forensic-redflag-checklist`, illustrates -> `insight:value-trap-patterns`, similar_to -> `case_study:vakrangee-manpasand`

`person:nick-sleep` | confidence: **verified** | tags: global, process, quality, compounding, low-turnover

Nomad Investment Partnership with Qais Zakaria (2001-2013/14): ~921% cumulative vs ~117% for MSCI World; ~20.8% a year net per one source vs ~6.5% for the index. Closed and returned capital in 2014 because they felt the work was done; partnership letters are public and widely studied. Early book: deep value in Asia/UK small caps; it evolved into a very concentrated portfolio of Amazon, Costco and Berkshire Hathaway (a German source says ~3 stocks at the end; uncorroborated). Process edge: 'destination analysis' - what will this business look like in 10-20 years - and the 'scale economies shared' model: firms that pass scale savings back to customers (Costco's low markups, Amazon's prices and free shipping) grow volume, which creates more scale savings, a flywheel competitors cannot match. Structural edge: an LP base and fee structure (performance fee over a hurdle, with deferral/clawback features - details unverified) that let them hold for a decade. Mistakes: Sleep wrote about errors of commission in early deep-value holdings and errors of omission (not sizing winners up sooner) - specifics unverified. Copyable: look for Indian companies that deliberately price low to widen the moat (DMart-style retail, low-cost brokers, platform businesses), judge them on customer value per rupee, and hold through quarterly noise.
